description: AstraMind is a Morocco-based team of five students passionate about AI, Data Science, Software Engineering, and Space Exploration. For NASA Space Apps 2026, we are tackling “Flame in Freefall” by turning microgravity combustion data into reliable fire-safety insights using AI/ML, data analysis, statistics, software, and visualization. We value collaboration, innovation, and building a strong prototype.
summary: FIREBRIDGE turns 26 years of NASA satellite fire detections into one record that can be compared across time. MODIS on Terra and Aqua is nearing the end of its mission while VIIRS on Suomi-NPP, NOAA-20 and NOAA-21 carries on, but the instruments see fire differently: 1 km versus 375 m pixels, different overpass hours, drifting orbits and a fleet that keeps changing. Raw counts jump when a satellite joins, not when fire changes. FIREBRIDGE archives 666,856,483 NASA FIRMS detections from all five satellites. Anyone can draw a place on the map and get its fire seasons, trends, weather drivers from NASA POWER, and an experimental sensor bridge that places every satellite on one Aqua-equivalent scale. Every satellite stays visible, and every finding is checked with statistical tests and cited fire science. An AI copilot explains results using only numbers computed in code. FIREBRIDGE helps researchers, fire managers and educators keep long-term fire trends honest through the MODIS-to-VIIRS transition.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

FIREBRIDGE is a web application for the "Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots" challenge. Pick a country, region or forest, or draw any area, choose dates, and FIREBRIDGE builds an analysis from every NASA FIRMS detection inside it:

- Overview: the whole record on one line, the satellite fleet as a stacked river, and findings in plain language.

- Fire seasons: each year as a ridgeline, so unusual seasons stand out.

- Fire drivers: daily NASA POWER weather (temperature, humidity, wind, rain) compared with fire activity.

- Sensor bridge: an experimental lab that estimates an Aqua-equivalent record from the years MODIS and VIIRS flew together (2012 to today), accounting for orbital drift. It is live but not independently validated, and every satellite stays visible beside it.

- Evidence: findings are tested against data they never used (Mann-Kendall trend test, Spearman correlation with permutation test, Rayleigh test for seasonality, chi-square) and compared with published fire science cited by DOI.

- Map, CSV export and SVG figures.

- A copilot that answers questions about an analysis. Facts are computed in code, the language model only phrases them, and every number in an answer is checked against those facts.

HOW IT WORKS

A data pipeline (Python, Apache Airflow, dbt, PostgreSQL/PostGIS) downloaded and audited the FIRMS archive: 666,856,483 records from Terra (since Nov 2000), Aqua (2002), Suomi-NPP (2012), NOAA-20 (2018) and NOAA-21 (2023). A TypeScript API and workers (Node.js, Prisma, Redis) serve the analyses. The frontend uses React, TypeScript, Vite, D3 and canvas. The copilot is a Python FastAPI service using open models on GroqCloud. Everything runs in Docker; GitHub Actions runs the tests, vulnerability scans and deployment. All code is open source (MIT).

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

When MODIS ends, long-term fire statistics risk a false jump: the VIIRS satellites hold about 4.7 times more archived detections than MODIS because of finer pixels, not more fire. FIREBRIDGE makes this visible and gives researchers, fire managers and educators a way to compare fire activity across the transition without hiding which satellite saw what.

CREATIVITY

Instead of hiding sensor differences, FIREBRIDGE shows them: the home page is a live Earth with the five satellites on their real orbit planes and scan swaths, and every result carries its own evidence. It states plainly what a detection is not: not a fire count, not burned area, and not proof that no fire burned.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Pixel size (1 km vs 375 m), overpass time (10:30 vs 13:30) and the drift of both MODIS satellites; satellites joining and leaving the record; clouds and data gaps; keeping unknown counts distinct from zero; the licence of every source; open-source code; plain language for non-specialists.

USE OF SUPER INTELLIGENCE (SI)

Code was written with SI coding assistants: Claude Code (Anthropic) for the web application and API, and OpenAI Codex for the data pipeline. The team directed, reviewed and tested all of it. The in-app copilot uses open language models (Qwen3.8 27B, gpt-oss) through GroqCloud to phrase explanations; numbers come from code, not the model. The presentation was assembled with SI assistance from real screenshots of the app. No SI-generated images, video or audio are used. Full list of sources and SI use: https://ogote.com/sources
